## Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is at the top of the agenda in the education field today, transforming the ways teachers and students learn, live, and work in technology-enriched environments across the globe. China, like many countries, has realized the changes that accompany educational technology and attached importance to cultivating modern students as digital citizens to adapt to the new era. The _Beijing Consensus on Artificial Intelligence and Education_ (UNESCO, 2019), which was released through an agreement by 50 government ministers, provides guidance on the reform of AI-integrated education for equitable and high-quality lifelong learning opportu- nities. The Ministry of Education in China (MOEC) has issued the “Action Plan for Artificial Intelligence Innovation in Universities” (MOEC, 2018), aimed at accelerating the novel application of AI in higher education, and using technology to support the innovation of university student training methods. These educational policies have highlighted the necessity of developing stu- dents’ AI-related knowledge and skills (Chai et  al., [2020;](#funding) Dai et  al., [2020)](#funding).

AI literacy has emerged as one of the essential competencies in higher education, influencing students to engage with and adapt to emerging technologies in academic and professional

pursuits (Kong et  al., 2021; Shang & Sivaparthipan, 2022). The primary cause is that AI tech- nologies have hastened the evolution of a highly automated society that reshapes the workforce, with a deep impact on the job market. This could be a massive challenge for university students preparing to enter the future labor market if they do not understand the technologies and principles of AI (Frey & Osborne, [2017)](#funding). This trend emphasizes the university’s pivotal respon- sibility to equip students with knowledge and skills to analyze, evaluate, and responsibly utilize AI tools, especially for future challenges in an AI-driven world (Katsantonis & Katsantonis, 2024; Kandlhofer et al., 2016). Thus, educators must take care in the evaluation of students’ AI literacy and design curricula based on AI literacy dimensions, which can prepare students to meet the demands of future labor market trends and increase their competitiveness for employment (Ng et  al., 2024; Zhang et  al., 2022).

A fundamental difference between AI and traditional computer science is that the former operates by mimicking human cognitive methods instead of simply using mechanical computation to make predictions and decisions, or solve specific problems (Akgun & Greenhow, [2022;](#funding) Celik, [2023)](#funding). Generative AI or machine learning techniques have significantly transformed the higher education landscape. For instance, particularly popular tools such as ChatGPT and IFlytek Spark, offer convincing advantages for building knowledge and understanding and completing assign- ments from the perspective of students (Celik, [2023;](#funding) Lund et al., 2023), but they may also raise issues of originality or academic integrity. A series of ethical issues or potential calculation biases caused by improper usage have been identified by researchers (Kong et al., 2023). AI’s powerful functions attract many university students to apply it, but the necessary literacy is required to maximize benefits and avoid potential risks. The lack of a suitable AI literacy standard could affect students’ values and creative thinking.

Therefore, an updated theoretical model of AI literacy is vital to ensure university students’ safe, effective, and normative use of this technology. A reliable measurement instrument is essential for identifying individual shortcomings and advantages in AI skills and knowledge, and for evaluating interventions that can improve AI literacy. Although some pioneers have estab- lished related assessments, most research has focused on the mastery of basic AI knowledge and skills, or emphasized learning intention or readiness, particularly in school contexts (Chai et al., [2020;](#funding) Dai et al., [2020;](#funding) Ng et al., 2023). A validated tool that considers university students’ growth features and development needs so as to comprehensively evaluate their AI literacy is much needed. This study aims to address the research gap by devising such a measurement for stu- dents in Chinese higher education, to assess their level of AI literacy and predict whether they can adapt to new technologies.

## Literature review

There have been many attempts to explore AI literacy’s connotation and scope, most of which agreed that it is still a long way from general knowledge to comprehensive literacy in the edu- cation field (Casal-Otero etc., [2023;](#funding) Ng et al., 2024). Existing literature confirmed that disruptive potential coexists alongside possible misuses when using digital technologies; it is therefore essential to start by understanding what AI literacy is to facilitate how AI functions for learning and social interaction (Kong et  al., 2023; Long & Magerko, 2020). Accordingly, we mainly reviewed the definition, measurements, and conceptual model of AI literacy. Although several efforts are being made to reveal the nature of AI literacy in Chinese literature (Chai et al., [2020;](#funding) Gong et  al., [2020)](#funding), there are still limited validated questionnaires with a clear theoretical foun- dation for university students.

### _The concept of AI literacy_

Concepts of AI literacy differ in the number of skill sets and competencies that are focused on. Literacy itself is a comprehensive idea that is not limited to ability, but covers an assortment 

JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON TECHNOLOGY IN EDUCATION 3

of facets combining knowledge, thinking, skills, emotions, attitudes, and other elements. Kandlhofer et  al. (2016) defined AI literacy as mastery over essential functions of AI applications in daily life and work, such as automata, intelligent agents, data structures, computational thinking, machine learning, deep learning, etc. Long and Magerko (2020) broadened the definition of AI literacy to abilities that allow individuals to critically assess and use AI technology, as well as effectively interact and communicate with AI tools. However, these definitions were not closely related to a particular educational context. A more categorical perspective proposed by Ng et al. (2021) referred to capabilities in four aspects, namely (1) knowing and understanding AI, (2) application of AI, (3) evaluation and creation of AI, and AI ethic. Even though their research initially revealed the level of requirements for students from the basic use, higher-order thinking, to human-centered considerations, it did not highlight the structural characteristics of literacy based on higher education.

Another common conceptualization of AI literacy is to replace “digital” in “digital literacy” with “AI” (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021). The term digital literacy is used to evaluate fundamental computer-related abilities to access and communicate information _via_ digital tech- nology (Falloon, [2020)](#funding). AI as intelligent machines and algorithms that can reason or adapt to rules or contexts by mimicking human intelligence; thus, its conceptual formation must consider additional proficiencies, such as emotion and behavior (Ng et al., 2023), ethical mindsets (Segun, 2021), communicative skills (Long & Magerko, 2020), etc. However, few studies have been found that provided detailed explanations on how to conceptualize AI literacy in higher education. On this basis, we defined university student AI literacy as an individual’s comprehensive capabilities and ethical values in obtaining AI knowledge, maintaining an open attitude, being aware of its implications, and applying techniques for current learning and future work in effective, norma- tive, and innovative ways.

### _Measuring AI literacy_

Several types of measurement instruments have been proposed in the educational field that were initial attempts to assess and cultivate students’ AI literacy. Kong et  al. (2021) designed an AI literacy course for university students and a self-reported survey (10 items) to track their improvement. Although this survey included three domains, namely AI concepts, applying con- cepts for evaluation, and applying concepts for solving problems, it ignored attitudinal and emotional aspects. Zhang et  al. (2022) implemented an AI literacy development workshop for middle school students and measured their literacy regarding general technical concepts, attitudes, career vision, and perceived ethical and societal implications. This was also a mixed-method study that considered both qualitative and quantitative data, and its focus was not only on the design of the evaluating tool. These studies emphasized measuring immediate and curriculum-specific learning outcomes in relation to AI courses, activities, or workshops, without addressing broader competencies that students need to effectively engage with AI in more gen- eralized contexts. This study can address this gap by introducing these underexplored dimensions, providing a more complete picture of AI literacy.

From a psychological competencies perspective, Carolus et al. ([2023)](#funding) proposed a self-assessment questionnaire to measure German adults’ AI literacy according to well-founded competency models and psychological change- and meta-competencies. Additionally, Ng et al. (2023) designed and validated the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (AILQ) using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Six factors were identified as literacy components among secondary students: intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, engagement, understanding, and application. Yet, existing scales developed for other groups are not suitable for university students, because they have different learning skills, ways of acquiring knowledge, and abilities required for entering into future work (Kandlhofer et al., 2016). It is thus necessary to explore and construct a measurement instrument on a theoretical basis and further validate it using empirical data in higher education.

### _Conceptual model of AI literacy_

According to Bloom’s Taxonomy, existing constructs of AI literacy (Ng et  al., 2021, 2023), and the current requirements for university students in China (MOEC, 2018), the conceptual frame- work of AI literacy consists of five dimensions ([Figure 1)](#conceptual-model-of-ai-literacy): (1) AI knowledge, (2) AI application, 

3. AI ethics, (4) AI attitude, and (5) AI innovation. The reason for using educational objectives Taxonomy as the theoretical basis is the necessity for the constructed framework to encapsulate the multifaceted developmental goals of AI literacy among university students. Aligning with this rationale, we designed a hierarchical structure that progresses from basic-order to higher-order literacy constructs. Thus, the proposed measurement tool could enhance its operationalizability and practical applicability in assessing the targeted population.

Associated with the structure of learning objectives in Bloom’s Taxonomy, knowledge refers to the remembering and understanding levels, as students must grasp core concepts and basic knowledge of AI, and understand operational principles like how neural networks function. Application links to the applying and analyzing levels, concerning students’ ability to apply AI tools and techniques, as well as higher-order analyzing skills to solve practical problems or perform specific tasks. Ethics relates to the evaluating level, since it serves to judge whether students can understand ethical implications and societal impacts, and use AI within moral and ethical bounds. In addition to meeting social norms of evaluation, attitude also connects to the evaluating level, considering personal acceptance, motivation, and self-evaluation. Innovation can represent the creating level, as modern students are expected to generate new ideas and solutions using the latest technology in practice.

AI knowledge is the cognition of the concepts and logic in the field of AI (Zhang et  al., 2022). Whereas knowing “what it is” is usually the first step for students in reaching new areas of learning. Thus, the most relevant studies designated knowledge as the most basic dimension to build AI literacy (Lee et  al., 2021). However, previous studies identified AI knowledge as knowing not only concepts, but also operating principles for interacting with AI tools or software (Laupichler et  al., 2023; Ng et  al., 2023). Moreover, some research highlighted discriminative ability, such as differentiating similar AI concepts and distinguishing AI tools from other digital

devices (Carolus et  al., [2023;](#funding) Wang et  al., 2023). Thus, three aspects, namely cognition of con- cept, working principles, and discrimination, were considered in this domain.

AI application refers to the skillful use of AI technology to solve problems in different sit- uations (Long & Magerko, 2020; Wang et al., 2023). It emphasizes the actual use and independent judgment of technology in study and life based on updated knowledge of current developments (Kong et  al., 2021), which is also a frequently included dimension in the conceptualization of AI competency. Previous research arguments concerning these skills can be classified into basic techniques in practice and behavior engagement, and higher-order usage in evaluation, collab- oration, and problem-solving (Carolus et  al., [2023;](#funding) Ng et  al., 2023; Wang et  al., 2023).

AI ethics is the ability to recognize ethical responsibilities and avoid risks and moral issues (Akgun & Greenhow, [2022;](#funding) Celik, [2023;](#funding) Jang et al., [2022)](#funding), and should be considered an important dimension of university students’ values regarding technology usage. Ethical consideration consists of a person’s capacities to comprehend the consequences of applying AI for society, and for other individuals (Zhang et  al., 2022). Frequently discussed ethical issues for users are integrity and plagiarism, intellectual property rights and legal liability, data privacy, and unfair decision-making caused by algorithm bias (Katsantonis & Katsantonis, 2024). Another point emphasized in the Chinese educational technology context is human-machine collaboration, in relation to the issue of limited human subjectivity (Shang & Sivaparthipan, 2022).

AI attitude refers to an individual’s feelings and beliefs regarding AI usage. It represents the willingness to accept AI and takes a particular role in influencing use behaviors (Katsantonis & Katsantonis, 2024). Researchers have been aware of the importance of attitude toward new technology for some time. For instance, Lin et  al. (2021) investigated students’ motivation to learn AI and demonstrated that affective learning can foster a mindset that influences how students approach it. Katsantonis and Katsantonis (2024) examined students’ AI attitudes and revealed that they display favorable motivational, emotional, and cognitive dispositions toward technology. We incorporated this dimension to explore how students emotionally and cognitively engage with AI technologies.

AI innovation requires students to have an experimental mindset and the capacity to apply technologies to deal creatively with real-world problems (Carolus et  al., [2023)](#funding), which is viewed as a type of higher-order literacy related to the critical thinking, problem-solving, and adapt- ability needed for the job market (Frey & Osborne, [2017)](#funding). This dimension is closely connected to the identity of the university student, who is at a stage that bridges study and society. A critical issue in Chinese higher education is that more curricula attention is paid to algorithmic principles in than learning how to innovatively employ AI (Li et  al., 2023). University students today are not just passive AI users, but active contributors to technological advancements, since they must prepare themselves for dynamic roles in an AI-driven world (Kong et  al., 2021). Therefore, we have included AI innovation as a construct of student’s AI literacy in higher education.

## Method

### _Research design_

The aim of this study is to develop a validated scale that is contextually suitable for assessing the AI literacy of university students in China. The research design consists of four steps ([Figure ](#item-generation) [2)](#item-generation): (1) conceptualization; (2) item generation; (3) structural model exploration; and 

4. scale validation. First, the conceptual framework of this study was determined through a review of literature that considered AI literacy, university student literacy characteristics, and the Chinese higher education context. Then, the initial items for the scale were generated, screened, and modified based on feedback from researchers in this field and university stu- dents. Subsequently, questionnaires from 386 respondents were collected for exploratory factor analysis (EFA), which was used to identify the underlying structure of items. Last, a data set 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

[**Figure 2.**](#method)[ ](#method)Research design.

of 401 respondents was collected for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), to further validate and evaluate the extent to which the factor structure obtained by the EFA interpreted an AI literacy framework.

### _Item generation_

The conceptual model of AI literacy we proposed above ([Figure 1)](#conceptual-model-of-ai-literacy) consists of five dimensions: 

1. AI knowledge, (2) AI ethics, (3) AI attitude, (4) AI application, and (5) AI innovation. On this basis, a series of sub-constructs and corresponding items were inspired, adapted, and screened to generate the initial scale. Combining existing measures can address the multifaceted nature of AI literacy and allow for building a more comprehensive assessment. Thus, we considered several validated scales from prior studies to capture diverse components, including the AI Literacy Questionnaire (AILQ) proposed by Ng et  al. (2023) (scale’s Cronbach’s α = 0.93), Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAIL) created by Carolus et al. ([2023)](#funding) (sub-scales’ Cronbach’s α = 0.66 − 0.93), the General Attitudes toward AI Scale (GAAIS) from Schepman and Rodway (2020)’s research (sub-scales’ Cronbach’s α = 0.74 − 0.87), and Wang et al. (2023) AI Literacy Scale (AILS) (sub-scales’ Cronbach’s α = 0.73 − 0.78).

Next, we invited three scholars in the educational technology field who were knowledgeable about this subject to evaluate the model’s accuracy, logicality, relevance, consistency, and repe- tition of expression to ensure content validity. The rationale for item inclusion was set based on the relevance to proposed dimensions, theoretically relevant cognitive levels, and the Chinese higher education context. For example, experts suggested that higher-order programming and computing skills should be removed because the structure is designed for students of all majors instead of computer science. In addition, we collected feedback from five university students who provided suggestions on the use of terms, reading, and comprehension issues that improved face validity. This process supported the modification of ambiguous items and the rephrasing of unclear expressions. Finally, 63 items within five dimensions were identified for the scale. A five-point Likert-type response was used as the assessment tool (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). The final version of the assessment is provided in [Appendix A.](#appendix-a-the-scale-of-al-literacy-for-chinese-university-students)

### _Population and sampling_

The population of the present research is public university students in China’s eastern coastal provinces, where the integration of AI into education is rapid and representative. We obtained informed consent from these universities after informing them of the research purpose, data use, and privacy protection measures. First, the inclusion of five universities was based on the research- ers’ convenience to ensure real and efficient data acquisition for the necessary sample size. Stratified random sampling was used in each participating university for diverse students’ grades and majors. The inclusion criteria for respondents were full-time undergraduate or postgraduate. We conducted

the survey online using Questionnaire Star, and set trap questions to the middle of the question- naire to ensure efficient data collection. Students participating in the questionnaire were volunteers and treated anonymously. A total of 450 questionnaires (50 in each province) were administered to university students; unusual (e.g., overly slow or quick response times; completely uniform choices) and uncompleted responses were excluded, and the remaining 386 valid samples were used for EFA. Likewise, we administered a further 450 questionnaires to university students, and received 401 valid samples for CFA. Both sample sizes are more than five times the number of items (_n_= 63) that meet the survey participant requirements (Gorsuch, [1983)](#funding).

Participating students’ demographics are shown in [Table 1.](#data-analysis) In both factor analysis groups, more female students (52.59%; 59.60%) than male students (47.41%; 40.40%) participated in the survey. Similar proportions of participants from the social science and engineering and science fields that covered most majors, which can provide students’ comprehensive perspective of new technology. Among the samples, data from 235 and 254 undergraduates were used for the two steps of factor analysis, while 151 and 147 graduates participated in the questionnaire for the two steps of data collection, respectively, which is consistent with the student structure of Chinese universities. The distribution of participants indicates a wide range of sample types.

### _Data analysis_

## Factor analysis was conducted using SPSS 26.0 and Amos 28.0 in this paper, which is a statistical approach widely used for creating structure and ensuring the rationality of items in research. In the EFA process, we employed the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett’s sphericity test to identify suitability for factor analysis, and principal-axis factoring (PAF) was used to extract the common factors. Parallel analysis and cumulative explained variance were used to determine the number of factors, and the strength and direction of the relationship between each variable and the factor. Then, we conducted a rotated component analysis using promax rotation to determine the factor structure and make it interpretable. In the phase of CFA, indi- cators like Standardized Root Mean-Squared Residual (SRMR), Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and Comparative Fit Index (CFI) were considered for measuring model fitting (Hu & Bentler, [1999)](#funding). Average variance extracted (AVE) and composite reliability (CR) values were assessed for the convergent validity, and the square root of a factor’s AVE for the discriminant validity. We calculated both Cronbach’s α and McDonald’s ω to measure the internal consistency of the questionnaire survey results comple- mentarily. Both inter-item and inter-dimension correlations were tested to determine whether this scale could be factor analyzed.

### _Exploratory factor analysis (EFA)_

EFA was conducted with an effective sample size of 386 to explore the essential dimension of the multivariate observed variables and achieve a more distinct explanation of items. Kaiser-Meyer- Olkin (KMO) test and Bartlett’s sphericity test were conducted to evaluate the adequacy of data in terms of sample size and item correlations. According to analytical results, the KMO score is 0.963, and Bartlett’s sphericity test is significant (_p_\< 0.05), which confirms these constructs are suitable for conducting EFA. Principal-axis factoring (PAF) is one of the most popular esti- mation methods in EFA that is appropriate for identifying underlying theoretical constructs by prioritizing common variance and excluding error variance (Fabrigar et  al., [1999)](#funding). Also, this analysis technique employs an iterative process to estimate factor loadings that contributes to more refined estimates of the interpretable structure (Widaman, 1993). Thus, we applied it as an extraction method to determine the structure.

By extracting common variance among items (Russell, 2002), we found that all factor loadings (above .40) retain factors with eigenvalues (above 1.00) at satisfactory scores. In addition, the matplotlib package in Python 3.9.18 was used to implement parallel analysis for this study. The factors corresponding to the true eigenvalues that are higher than the average eigenvalues of the random matrix would be retained, which shows these factors are sufficiently explanatory. A five-factor construct was determined for interpretative items: (i) it is conceptually supported by the existing evidence, (ii) the total cumulative variance interpretation is 65.360%, which is acceptable ([Table 3)](#exploratory-factor-analysis-efa), and (iii) the number of factors higher than the average eigenvalue of the random matrix is five in the scree plot ([Figure 3)](#confirmatory-factor-analysis-cfa).

Rotated component analysis results ([Table 4)](#confirmatory-factor-analysis-cfa) confirmed five significant constructs across all items. The pattern coefficients of all items were higher than 0.7 (Hair et  al., [2010)](#funding), and the classification was consistent with the proposed conceptual framework, showing satisfactory cor- respondence between the proposed items and the factors. Five factors were named: (1) AI knowledge (KN, 13 items), (2) AI ethics (ET, 14 items), (3) AI attitude (AT, 13 items), (4) AI application (AP, 18 items), and (5) AI innovation (IN, 5 items).

### _Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)_

### In the CFA process, 401 valid samples were analyzed to evaluate the construct validity, conver- gent validity, and discriminant validity of the AI literacy model, meeting the minimal sample size requirements (_n_ \> 100) (Bollen, [1989)](#funding). This study adopted commonly used criteria to examine 

the observed fitting indicators and verify the structural validity of the measurement model. Specifically, SRMR is 0.028 and RMSEA is 0.032, which are both lower than 0.05 and thus meet the requirements. The values of CFI and TLI are 0.979 and 0.978, respectively, both above 0.9 (Bentler, [1990)](#funding). The other indexes of model fit (PCMIN/DF, NFI, IFI, PCFI, etc.) shown in Table 5, prove that the new AI literacy model has good construct validity. The structure of the first-order model of AI literacy is presented in Figure 4.

A measurement model with good convergent validity illustrates a high degree of correlation between measured items of the same latent factors, which can accurately reflect the properties of the latent factors. According to the reasonable ranges of the indexes for: factor loadings (\>0.70), the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) (\>0.50), and Composite Reliability (CR) (\>0.70) (Hair et  al., [2010)](#funding), results indicated strong internal correlations among all items and their cor- responding factors (Table 6). The minimum factor loading is 0.764, while the maximum value is 0.830. Meanwhile, the minimum of AVE and CR are 0.616 and 0.889, respectively, demon- strating that this model has good convergent validity. Table 6 shows all correlations and the square root of AVE. The dimensions’ square roots of AVE are 0.790, 0.825, 0.816, 0.797, and

## Discussion

This study developed an AI literacy model for university students that was theoretically con- nected to the structure of educational goals. Using two-step factor analysis, we were able to demonstrate the reliability and validity of the structure that involves five distinct constructs, namely AI knowledge, application, ethics, attitude, and innovation. These components of AI literacy do not adhere to a strict hierarchical order, but they are strongly laterally connected. The results indicated that most dimensions verified here are aligned with previous scales (Carolus et  al., [2023;](#funding) Laupichler et  al., 2023; Ng et  al., 2023). Differently, the domain of AI innovation has been added, the reason could be the specific requirements of the university context, con- sistent with arguments that literacy models must shed light on the knowledge and skills needed to creatively apply AI (Kong et  al., 2021; Lin et  al., 2021).

Knowledge and application are basic components in most AI literacy models (Ng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022). Likewise, this study valued AI knowledge and AI application as indispensable foundational elements for equipping students with the information needed to navigate the com- plex landscape of AI technologies. This required the development of AI education as a general course in higher education (Katsantonis & Katsantonis, 2024; Kong et al., 2021). The evaluation of AI application served to assess how students utilize their AI knowledge to solve problems and finish tasks, which can promote their ethical, optimized, and effective usage of such tools. We viewed the design of these evaluation details as a starting point that can offer a reference for designing the curriculum’s objectives.

Consistent with the findings in some studies (Celik, [2023;](#funding) Ng et  al., 2023), AI ethics must be a sub-scale in evaluating AI literacy, since it protects ideological security to ensure reasonable and sustainable utilization. It is crucial to foster appropriate values among students using AI. However, the complexity of this concept led to a lack of sufficient prior knowledge or a limited ability to engage with the ethical challenges (Akgun & Greenhow, [2022;](#funding) Segun, 2021). A common concern is that generative AI language models are popular among university students, but many of them often ignore moral and legal issues (e.g., data reliability, copyright, and accountability) (Lund et  al., 2023). Thus, more effort should be put into reminding students how to use and evaluate AI responsibly and morally in their studies and lives.

Compared to common emotional constructs, like individual acceptance of and anxiety toward AI technology (Schepman & Rodway, 2020; Wang & Wang, 2022), this scale extended the range of AI attitudes by adding subjective reasons and motivation for students’ optimistic or negative attitudes toward new technology from a psychological perspective. Given the potential ethical issues (e.g., plagiarism) and risks (e.g., over-reliance on machines), the breadth and depth of AI integration into higher education is controversial (Lin et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022). Therefore, examining students’ attitudes and reasons behind students’ opinions, such as motivation and self-efficiency, is necessary.

Different from several existing models where AI innovation is not explicitly mentioned (Laupichler et  al., 2023; Ng et  al., 2023), this study first identified AI innovation as a separate 

JOURNAL OF RESEARCH ON TECHNOLOGY IN EDUCATION 13

sub-scale, showing the importance of creative thinking and behaviors in Chinese higher educa- tion. In line with other Chinese research (Chai et  al., [2020;](#funding) Dai et  al., [2020)](#funding), innovative ability is one of the most critical goals of high-quality talent training and man-machine collaboration. The primary reason was that the nature of AI requires individuals to apply it in flexible and innovative ways (Kandlhofer et  al., 2016; Li et  al., 2023). Although Carolus et  al. ([2023)](#funding) iden- tified “Create AI” in AI literacy, our findings subdivided innovative awareness and innovative action based on this.

## Implications and limitations

This article contributes to building a comprehensive structure that clearly defines components of AI literacy and can be used to evaluate university students’ levels and progress. By encom- passing a wide range of information, this scale can improve clarity for respondents and facilitate a more intricate analysis of complex constructs. This newly developed assessment can inform related instructional strategies, curriculum design, and the integration of competencies into the university setting. For instance, effective measurement enables educators to tailor teaching approaches that address students’ understanding of AI concepts, skills, and ethical considerations. In terms of theoretical implications, it verifies the suitability of the assessment framework to educational objectives taxonomy, which functions as a theoretical basis for the categorical objec- tives of AI education content.

The research limitation might lie in contextual generalizability since the current data was collected from five representative Chinese universities. Further adaptability of the model is suggested by generalizing the results of students from more universities and regions. If there are contextual differences, cross-cultural comparative analysis regarding AI literacy is therefore necessary. In addition, qualitative research approaches are suggested to address these questions in more depth and uncover explanations behind students’ AI application behaviors and their attitudes toward the rapid iteration of AI technology. We could conduct longitudinal studies in the future, which can continually improve the understanding and update the model of AI literacy to keep up with the rapid development of AI technology.

## Conclusion

Education in the AI era must equip students with literacy in the use of educational technology needed to enrich their learning opportunities, pursue their careers, facilitate their work effec- tiveness, and cultivate them as responsible digital citizens. This study provides an updated model of AI literacy and a five-factor assessment scale for university students by reconstructing its conceptualization, which advances the research field of AI integration into higher education. We offer the first validated measurement tool across multifaceted indexes grounded in the theoretical perspective of educational objective classification for Chinese universities, which could be an adaptable model for assessing AI literacy in diverse cultural contexts. The results underscore the importance of integrating ethics, attitudes, and innovation into AI literacy assessments, expanding beyond knowledge-based and technical application approaches. It contributes to quantifying the evaluation criteria that examine whether students have the capacity to use AI effectively. This article has practical implications for policymakers in designing targeted inventions and for university educators in using the information to assess students’ AI literacy development and adjust corresponding cultivating programs to improve AI literacy.

### [Appendix A. ](#item-generation) The scale of Al literacy for Chinese university students

AI Knowledge

1. I know what AI is.
2. I can understand basic AI knowledge.
3. I can name the strengths and weaknesses of AI.
4. I can explain why AI has become increasingly important.
5. I know some working principles behind AI, like decision trees and natural language processing.
6. I can describe how biases arise in AI systems.
7. I understand how AI receives information and interacts with people to handle various tasks.
8. I understand the reasoning and decision-making processes of AI technologies.
9. I can tell the differences between similar AI concepts, such as deep learning, machine learning, and reinforcement learning.
10. I can tell if I am dealing with an application based on AI.
11. I can distinguish devices that use AI from devices that do not.
12. I can distinguish if I am interacting with AI or humans.
13. I can distinguish the differences between assignments done by interactive AI and those done by humans. AI Ethics
14. I think that AI ethics is important to guide AI applications.
15. I think that the misuse of AI can cause potential risks.
16. I agree with being alert to the abuse of AI technologies.
17. When using the data or information provided by AI platforms, I consider the ethical issues.
18. I think that users should be responsible for considering AI design and decision processes.
19. I know potential legal problems that may arise when using AI.
20. I think AI systems should meet ethical and legal standards.
21. I think AI systems need to be rigorously tested.
22. I think AI systems should minimize bias over data, like gender and ethnicity.
23. I think that AI systems should respect privacy.
24. I can describe the role of humans in the development of AI systems.
25. I can describe the potential impacts of AI on individuals and society.
26. I agree with the people-centered principle when using AI.
27. I can prevent an AI from influencing me in my decisions. AI Attitude
28. There are many benefits of using AI applications.
29. AI can provide new opportunities for study.
30. I think some complex decisions are best left to the AI system.
31. I think AI has enriched human study, work, and life.
32. I think AI can promote human development.
33. I learn AI because it is related to my study and work content.
34. Learning AI applications is interesting.
35. I am curious about discovering new AI technologies.
36. Learning AI applications makes my life more meaningful.
37. I am confident in my performance on AI-related tasks and projects.
38. I believe I can master AI knowledge and skills.
39. I believe I can achieve good grades in AI-related assessments. AI Application
40. Learning AI applications is not very difficult for me.
41. I can use AI applications to make my daily study easier.
42. I can use AI to achieve my daily goals.
43. I can find AI resources to support my study.
44. I can skillfully use AI applications to help my daily study and life.
45. I can choose AI tools to complete complex tasks.
46. I can comprehensively evaluate AI’s functions after usage.
47. I can critically evaluate the implications of AI applications in a certain subject area.
48. I can choose a proper solution from various solutions provided by AI.
49. I actively participate in AI learning activities.
50. I take initiatively to collect AI learning materials.
51. I learn effectively in AI-related learning tasks.
52. I often try to explain AI applications to my classmates.
53. I am willing to work with my classmates to complete AI learning tasks and projects.
54. I often spend my spare time discussing AI with my classmates.
55. I usually ask classmates for help when encountering difficulties in AI activities.
56. I can choose the appropriate AI tools based on actual problems.
57. I can use AI technologies to create an intelligent environment for complex problems.
58. I can use AI devices to expand cognition when dealing with complicated tasks. AI Innovation
59. I can keep myself updated with the latest innovations in AI applications.
60. I can use AI applications to find out innovative solutions to problems.
61. I will continue to use AI innovatively in the future.
62. I plan to explore new features of AI applications in the future.
63. I can imagine possible future uses of AI.
